chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from al-Ya'qubi, from Musa ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Mayasarah, from Abu al-Jahm, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said:

"If a man stole a thousand dirhams and used them to buy a female slave or gave her as dowry to a woman, then the private part (consummation) is permissible for him, but he bears the liability (debt/restitution) for the money."

The book of Divorce has ended. 'And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.' * And may Allah bless Muhammad and his family, and the book of Manumission, Manumission by Stipulation, and Manumission by Agreement will follow, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
ai.seo_question: Is consummation with a female slave purchased with stolen money permissible in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This ruling from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that the validity of consummation (istimta') with a female slave acquired via stolen funds is not invalidated by the theft itself, as the slave becomes his property, though the financial debt remains. This distinction highlights the Shia juristic principle separating the right of possession from the obligation of restitution, a key nuance in *fiqh al-malikiyya*. The placement at the end of the Book of Divorce underscores the interplay between marital rights and property law in classical legal compilations.
